title: The Anandpur resolution, 1973
hookLine: the Akali Dal set out demands for Punjab's rights, read very differently by different people

lines: A FAIR ASK, OR A WARNING?
cards: One document, two readers. The first reads it and sees a fair request: let a state run more of its own affairs. The second sees a warning sign: the start of breaking away.
They may even be holding the same pages. What differs is the fear each brings to them.
In the year in today's title, the Akali Dal met at Anandpur Sahib, the town where the Khalsa was born, and set down what it wanted for Punjab.
That document is the Anandpur resolution, and how people read it shaped the years that followed.

teach.b: First, the place. Anandpur Sahib is where tradition says Guru Gobind Singh called the Khalsa into being. Meeting there tied the demands to the heart of the panth's story.
Second, what it asked. Histories summarize it like this.
The central government should keep a short list of powers, such as defense, foreign affairs and currency, and leave the rest to the states. Chandigarh should go to Punjab.
Punjab's share of the river waters should be settled fairly. And it set out religious and social aims for the Sikhs as well. Third, the two readings.
Akali leaders said it was about federalism: more say for every state, not just Punjab, inside India. Critics in Delhi and elsewhere read it as a step toward a separate Sikh country.
It didn't help that more than one version of the text went around, and people quoted the version that fit their fear. Historians still describe it in different ways. Fourth, the root.
At Ang 97 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says that all are partners in the Lord's care, and no one is outside it. A partner's voice is worth hearing in full, before it's labeled.
When one text is read two ways, the work is to find out what each reader is afraid of.

how: The Anandpur Sahib resolution is still debated in Punjab politics; Akali leaders have described it as a call for federalism, and historians present its different readings and versions side by side.

games.q: a friend sends you one quote from the resolution, with an angry caption. what do you do?
o: share it: the quote speaks for itself.
find which version it came from and how each side reads it.
games.why: more than one version went around, and each side quoted the one that fit. reading both sides starts with knowing which text you're holding.

practice: Choose one argument, in your life or in the news, where you already know whose side you're on.
Breathe in and say, as fairly as you can, what your side wants and what it fears; breathe out and say what the other side wants and fears, in words they would recognize.
You don't have to change your mind, only hear both, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru at the end.
